findings.quote: most serious reactions come from mismatched blood, and cross-matching is designed to catch this
findings.explanation: Contradicts the same page: risks[1] calls fluid overload "the commonest serious harm", and steps[0] says most incompatible transfusions come from clerical or identification errors, which laboratory cross-matching cannot detect (wrong blood in tube, bedside mix-ups). UK haemovigilance (SHOT) attributes most serious harm to transfusion-associated circulatory overload and process errors, not to laboratory mismatch; ABO-incompatible transfusion is rare.
findings.suggestedFix: Say the laboratory checks the sample against donor units for compatibility, and that the most serious avoidable harm is giving the wrong unit to the wrong patient, hence strict sample labelling and bedside identity checks. Drop the claim that most serious reactions come from mismatched blood.

findings.quote: Most people who follow their rehabilitation programme resume nearly all normal activities within about three to six weeks
findings.explanation: Contradicts the first sentence of the same field (walking without aids by about six weeks, driving at 6-8 weeks, most of the benefit by three months, improvement for a year). Nearly all normal activities by 3-6 weeks is unrealistic after a major joint operation and sets false expectations; at six weeks most people are still in rehabilitation with swelling and limited bend.
findings.suggestedFix: Delete the sentence, or say many people manage most light daily activities within a few weeks and reach most of the benefit by about three months.

findings.quote: Infected skin (cellulitis) over the planned entry point is the one absolute contraindication
findings.explanation: Incomplete and potentially misleading. The 'what' field says aspiration is "often followed by an injection of corticosteroid", and nowhere does the page say steroid must not be injected when the joint itself may be infected. A hot swollen joint of unknown cause is aspirated first; steroid is withheld until infection is reasonably excluded (suspected septic arthritis, bacteraemia, intra-articular fracture and joint replacements are also reasons not to inject or to leave the procedure to the orthopaedic team). 'The one absolute contraindication' is true only for needle entry.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a sentence that corticosteroid is not injected if infection is suspected and is given only after infection has been reasonably excluded; reword 'the one absolute contraindication' to 'the main contraindication to needle entry'; note that aspiration of a prosthetic joint is normally left to the orthopaedic team.

findings.quote: a severe headache with visual disturbance, calf pain or breathlessness are reported to the maternity unit or NHS 111 straight away
findings.explanation: Under-triages emergencies. After caesarean, breathlessness or chest pain (pulmonary embolism), very heavy bleeding with faintness (secondary postpartum haemorrhage) and severe headache with visual disturbance (postpartum pre-eclampsia, eclampsia, stroke) are leading causes of maternal death and need 999 or the emergency department, not NHS 111. Other pages in this slice already do this (knee-replacement: "chest pain or breathlessness is an emergency").
findings.suggestedFix: Split the line: call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, breathlessness, a fit or collapse, very heavy bleeding or severe headache with visual disturbance; contact the maternity unit or NHS 111 the same day for fever, offensive discharge, wound redness or discharge, calf pain or swelling.

findings.quote: Standing urination follows successful urethral lengthening and penetrative sex follows an erectile implant.
findings.explanation: Reads as a guaranteed outcome. Erectile implants after phalloplasty have high complication and revision rates (infection, erosion or extrusion, mechanical failure, removal in a substantial minority) and not everyone achieves satisfactory penetrative sex. Urethral lengthening is itself complicated by fistula or stricture in a large proportion; the risk list names these as 'the commonest complications' and implant problems but gives no sense of how often. The implant clause has no qualifier.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword, for example: 'An erectile implant can make penetrative sex possible for some people, but implant complications and further operations are common; many people can urinate standing after urethral lengthening, though fistula or stricture often needs revision.' Add a frequency range only from a cited surgical review.

findings.quote: Stroke, heart attack, arrhythmia, perforation of the heart (all rare, well under 1%)
findings.explanation: The figure fits diagnostic coronary angiography, but the page also covers electrophysiology studies and ablation (aliases, what, why, steps). For catheter ablation, especially for atrial fibrillation, cardiac perforation or tamponade is reported at roughly 0.5-1.5%, stroke or TIA at a few tenths of a per cent to about 1%, and major complications overall at a few per cent, plus items not listed (phrenic nerve injury, pulmonary vein stenosis, rare atrio-oesophageal fistula). Only pacemaker-needing conduction damage is listed for ablation. The 'what' field's 'very safe in experienced hands' generalises the same way.
findings.suggestedFix: Restrict the 'well under 1%' wording to diagnostic angiography and give ablation its own risk line from an EHRA/ESC or BHRS source, or remove ablation and electrophysiology from the aliases and point readers to specialist information.

findings.quote: Stop acid-suppressing tablets for two weeks if testing for H. pylori or ulcers is the aim
findings.explanation: Worded as an instruction to stop a medicine. Only H. pylori testing (breath, stool antigen or biopsy) needs acid suppression such as a PPI paused about two weeks beforehand, to avoid false negatives. Looking for ulcers does not, and stopping acid suppression in someone with a suspected ulcer, bleeding, Barrett oesophagus or severe reflux can do harm. The endoscopy unit decides for each person.
findings.suggestedFix: Say that if H. pylori testing is planned the unit may ask the person to pause acid-suppressing medicines for about two weeks beforehand, and that they should do this only on the unit's instruction. Remove 'or ulcers'.

findings.quote: No driving for 24 hours; results in a week or two
findings.explanation: The after-care list has no warning-sign signposting, although risks lists bleeding, pneumothorax (a few per cent after transbronchial biopsy) and infection. These can declare themselves after discharge as increasing breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up more than streaks of blood or fever. The gastroscopy and colonoscopy pages carry such a line; this one does not.
findings.suggestedFix: Add: increasing breathlessness, chest pain, coughing up more than streaks of blood, or fever after the test need urgent assessment (999 or emergency department); a little blood-streaked sputum for a day is expected.

findings.quote: Steroid or hyaluronic acid injections
findings.explanation: UK-first site, but NICE NG226 (osteoarthritis, 2022) advises against offering intra-articular hyaluronan injections and positions corticosteroid injection as an adjunct for short-term relief. Listing hyaluronic acid as a standard alternative reflects US practice presented as general.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'corticosteroid injections for short-term relief' and either drop hyaluronic acid or add that NICE does not recommend it.

findings.quote: pelvic-girdle
findings.explanation: The linked organs are 'Bony pelvis' and 'Foot' (organs: pelvic-girdle, foot). Neither is part of a knee replacement, while organs.json already has a 'knee' (Knee joint) organ whose match names include the femur, tibia and patella listed in structures. Same omission in joint-aspiration, whose organs are pelvic-girdle, shoulder-girdle and hand although the knee is described as the commonest site.
findings.suggestedFix: Set organs to ["knee"] on knee-replacement and add "knee" to joint-aspiration.

findings.quote: a hot or painful calf, breathlessness, or difficulty passing urine are reported to the surgical team or to NHS 111 without waiting for the follow-up appointment
findings.explanation: Same under-triage as the caesarean page. Breathlessness or chest pain after pelvic surgery may be pulmonary embolism and heavy or fresh bleeding may need emergency care; the page lists venous thromboembolism among its risks but sends all of these to the surgical team or NHS 111 rather than 999.
findings.suggestedFix: Call 999 or go to A&E for chest pain, breathlessness or very heavy bleeding; contact the surgical team or NHS 111 the same day for fever, offensive discharge, a hot painful calf or difficulty passing urine.

findings.quote: bleeding after polyp removal can be delayed by up to a week
findings.explanation: Delayed post-polypectomy bleeding is usually described as occurring up to about two weeks after the procedure (occasionally later), not one week. The same shorter window appears in risks[0] ('sometimes delayed by a week'). A person bleeding on day 8-14 could think it unrelated and not seek help.
findings.suggestedFix: Change to 'up to about two weeks' here and in risks[0].

findings.quote: Local anaesthetic to the wrist or groin, light sedation; awake throughout
findings.explanation: True of diagnostic angiography, not of the electrophysiology and ablation procedures the page also covers. Catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation (and some valve or structural procedures such as TAVI) is commonly done under general anaesthesia or deep sedation and takes several hours, against the 'half an hour and an hour' quoted in 'what'. The 'what' field makes the same generalisation ("The person is awake ... and can follow instructions during the test").
findings.suggestedFix: Qualify as 'for coronary angiography' and add that ablation and valve procedures may need general anaesthesia or deep sedation and take longer.

findings.quote: Stop clopidogrel a few days before; continue aspirin
findings.explanation: Phrased as an unqualified instruction to stop a medicine. Many people having bypass surgery have recent stents or an acute coronary syndrome, where stopping a P2Y12 inhibitor without the team's direction risks stent thrombosis (the angioplasty page says exactly this). Timing is drug-specific and set by the surgical team (roughly 3-7 days depending on ticagrelor, clopidogrel or prasugrel), not 'a few days' for everyone.
findings.suggestedFix: Reword: the surgical team tells the person when to stop clopidogrel or another second antiplatelet before surgery (the interval depends on the drug) and it should not be stopped without their instruction; aspirin is usually continued.

findings.quote: Antibiotics continued for a few days if the appendix had perforated
findings.explanation: The after-care list has no 'when to seek help' item, although the page names pelvic or intra-abdominal abscess, wound infection and stump leak as risks. These typically present days to two weeks after discharge with worsening abdominal pain, fever, vomiting or a red, swollen or discharging wound. Most other surgical pages in this slice carry such a line.
findings.suggestedFix: Add: worsening abdominal pain, fever, persistent vomiting, or a wound that becomes red, swollen or discharges should be reported to the surgical team, NHS 111 or the emergency department the same day.

findings.quote: Follow-up at about six to eight weeks, with an ECG or echocardiogram to check how the heart is working
findings.explanation: No warning-sign signposting for a major operation. Sternal wound infection or instability (discharge, clicking, fever), new chest pain, breathlessness, palpitations (the page says atrial fibrillation affects about a third), calf swelling and leg-wound infection all warrant contact with the cardiac team or urgent care before the six-week review.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a bullet: contact the cardiac surgical team or NHS 111 the same day for wound redness, discharge or a moving breastbone, fever, palpitations or leg swelling; call 999 for chest pain or severe breathlessness.

findings.quote: The tissue removed is sent for examination under the microscope; an unexpected abnormality is uncommon but is followed up in the usual way
findings.explanation: After-care has no red-flag signposting even though risks[0] calls haematoma "the main early complication". A rapidly enlarging tense swelling or one-sided pain (may need return to theatre), a dusky nipple graft, fever or spreading redness, calf pain or breathlessness need same-day contact with the surgical team or the emergency department. The page also never says to go back to the operating unit rather than a local service.
findings.suggestedFix: Add a bullet naming these warning signs and directing readers to the surgical team, NHS 111 or 999 as appropriate.

findings.quote: NHS: Appendicitis treatment
findings.explanation: Title says 'treatment' but the URL (https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/appendicitis/) is the NHS appendicitis overview page; the treatment page sits under /treatment/. Neither named reference plausibly supports specific claims on the page such as 'about a third need surgery within a few years' on antibiotics alone or 'full recovery often takes around two weeks on average'.
findings.suggestedFix: Point the URL at the treatment page or retitle it 'NHS: Appendicitis'; add the trial source for the antibiotic-failure figure or soften it.

findings.quote: Erotic sensation and orgasm are usually retained because the clitoris is preserved at the base.
findings.explanation: An outcome claim stated as the expected result with a causal explanation. Published series report ability to orgasm in most but not all people, with variable reporting, and a minority describe reduced or lost sensation. None of the four references (WPATH SOC8, UCSF primary-care guidelines, NHS gender dysphoria page, WHO ICD FAQ) contains surgical outcome data, and the technique-level statements in steps (flap vessels, nerve coaptation) likewise rest on no surgical source.
findings.suggestedFix: Soften to 'Most people report being able to orgasm after surgery, but sensation varies and is not guaranteed', and add a surgical outcomes review as a reference, or remove the sentence.

findings.quote: Regret, which is reported to be rare
findings.explanation: Listed as a risk but worded as reassurance, with no source: the page's references are WPATH SOC8, UCSF guidelines, an NHS overview, a gov.uk screening leaflet and a WHO FAQ, none giving regret data. Published adult series report low regret (about 1% or less), but follow-up is often short and incomplete, which the sentence omits; for neutrality it should be sourced and caveated.
findings.suggestedFix: Say 'Regret is reported by a small minority of people in published studies, although many studies have short or incomplete follow-up' and cite a systematic review, or delete it from the risk list.

notes: No finding is rated high: I found no outright wrong anatomy, dose or technique, and the content is generally careful, with good red-flag lines on most pages. The four gender-affirming pages (chest-masculinisation, phalloplasty, vaginoplasty, plus the inclusive wording in hysterectomy and caesarean-section) are accurate and neutral: the WHO ICD-11 statement is correct, techniques and complications are described correctly (including fertility, hair removal, oestrogen and VTE, screening and PSA caveats), and outcome promises are limited to the three items flagged (phalloplasty implant and orgasm wording, vaginoplasty regret). Their technique-level detail (flap pedicles, nerve coaptation, canal planes, which complications are commonest) is not backed by any named reference (WPATH SOC8, UCSF, NHS, gov.uk and WHO are overview or guideline sources), so a peer-reviewed surgical review should be added for a specialist to verify. More than 20 candidate points were found; the 20 above are kept and the rest are listed here, so no entity is marked clean: cholecystectomy, cataract-surgery, angioplasty, dialysis and urinary-catheterization have no reported finding, only these low-priority points. (1) Unsupported superlatives: cataract-surgery.what 'it is the commonest operation in the world', cholecystectomy.what 'The commonest planned abdominal operation', urinary-catheterization.what 'the commonest healthcare-associated infection'; each is safer as 'one of the commonest' (some UK point-prevalence surveys have ranked respiratory infection above urinary infection). (2) angioplasty.after[1] says mild chest discomfort in the first days 'is often the stent settling', and after[4] lists 'severe chest pain' under 'contact the unit or seek urgent help'; chest pain like the original symptoms should say 999. (3) dialysis.risks[2] lists peritoneal dialysis peritonitis warning signs (pain, fever, cloudy fluid) but never says to contact the PD unit the same day. (4) appendectomy.recovery: 'recover from keyhole surgery within a couple of weeks, although ... full recovery often takes around two weeks on average' is redundant and sits oddly with 'sport in two to four weeks'; appendectomy.after[2] gives shoulder-tip pain 'up to a week' but cholecystectomy.after[1] says 'a day or two'. (5) joint-aspiration.references: 'NHS: Steroid injections' points to the generic /medicines/steroids/ page and the Cambridge leaflet is about children having a joint injection under general anaesthetic, so neither supports the adult aspiration claims (for example 'limit to 3-4 a year'); recovery says steroid benefit 'builds over a few days' and also 'acts quickly'. (6) cholecystectomy.why[4] biliary dyskinesia as an indication is nearer US than UK practice; cholecystectomy anatomy.structures lists caudate lobe and common hepatic artery (not what is dissected; the cystic artery arises from the right hepatic artery) and colonoscopy lists 'Sigmoid artery' rather than sigmoid colon; cross-link lists on cataract-surgery (symptoms: headache; related: knee-replacement) look loosely generated. (7) cardiac-catheterization.why[0] calls angiography 'the definitive test' while its own alternatives list CT coronary angiography, which NICE favours first for stable chest pain. (8) hysterectomy.what 'The fallopian tubes are usually removed' is safer as 'often'. Could not verify offline: reference URLs and the content of the PMC, StatPearls, MedlinePlus and NHS pages (for example MedlinePlus patientinstructions/000375 and ency/article/007256, and the NHS 'gender-dysphoria-and-incongruence' URL); I judged only title and URL coherence and plausibility. Figures that looked right and were not flagged include the STEMI 120-minute target, bile duct injury about 1 in 300, deep knee infection about 1%, CABG death 1-2% and stroke 1-2%, gastroscopy perforation about 1 in 3000, peritoneal dialysis peritonitis one episode per 2-3 years, and DVLA-consistent driving advice after CABG.
